about.title: People of the World Wide Web, 1945 to 2026
about.description: Who worked where and when, how they were tied to each other, and which idea led to which product. Compiled from Tim Berners-Lee's memoir This Is for Everyone (2025), written with Stephen Witt, with careers the book does not date checked on the web and linked. It is one participant's account.
about.author: Raffael Schneider

fields.people[].stints: one role at one organisation: org, role, start, end (null while ongoing or not known to have ended), place, left, src, ref (chapter) or url
fields.links: ties between two people: kind, date, note, src, ref
fields.moments: kind idea, product or event: id, date, title, short, detail, people, orgs, track (ideas and products), src, ref or url
fields.dates: YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD; precision as given by the source
fields.tracks: the fields ideas and products are sorted into, in display order
fields.paradigms: eras of the web, which overlap
fields.lineage: which idea or product led to which: from, to (moment ids), note, src, ref

paradigms.name: Hypertext before the web
paradigms.summary: Bush, Nelson and Engelbart imagined linked documents, though Berners-Lee says he had not heard of them when he first thought of the web.

paradigms.name: One web, given away
paradigms.summary: A proposal at CERN, a working system on a NeXT machine, and the decision to put the technology in the public domain.

paradigms.name: Browsers and the boom
paradigms.summary: Mosaic brought pictures, Netscape and Microsoft fought over the browser, and the money arrived and crashed.

paradigms.name: Standards by consortium
paradigms.summary: W3C and its members agree the web's formats, with a royalty-free patent policy and a split over HTML along the way.

paradigms.name: Platforms
paradigms.summary: Search and social networks gathered the web's activity, and its data, in a few places.

paradigms.name: The mobile web
paradigms.summary: The phone becomes the main way to reach the web, and apps compete with it.

paradigms.name: Open data
paradigms.summary: Governments are pressed to publish raw data, from Data.gov.uk to the Open Data Institute.

paradigms.name: Data sovereignty
paradigms.summary: Solid and its pods try to give people back control of their own data.

paradigms.name: The attention economy
paradigms.summary: Microtargeting and engagement algorithms become a public worry after Brexit and the 2016 US election.

paradigms.name: Intelligent machines
paradigms.summary: Models trained on the web's text reach the public through ChatGPT.

moments.title: Bush imagines link trails between documents
moments.detail: An Atlantic article by Vannevar Bush described non-linear retrieval and associative trails, and called for an electromechanical Memex.

moments.title: UN human rights declaration
moments.detail: The stated inspiration for the Contract for the Web.
moments.ref: Chapter 14: The Contract for the Web

moments.title: Ferranti Mark 1 computer in use
moments.detail: The parents of Berners-Lee met around 1950 working on this early commercial computer, which Turing also used.

moments.title: Turing proposes the Imitation Game
moments.detail: A paper imagined a machine whose conversation could not be told apart from that of a person.

moments.title: Nelson coins hypertext for Project Xanadu
moments.detail: Nelson envisioned a universal, centrally run information space with two-way links. It never passed the prototype stage.

moments.title: Engelbart demonstrates the mouse and the hyperlink
moments.detail: A ninety-minute San Francisco presentation showed collaborative editing, teleconferencing, the mouse and links on a single computer.

moments.title: File Transfer Protocol
moments.detail: The usual way to fetch files from another computer before the web; slow, with a separate connection each time.

moments.title: Rouse walks Berners-Lee through public-key cryptography
moments.detail: On a 1977 coastal walk Paul Rouse explained the recent Rivest, Shamir and Adelman paper. The book dates the walk, not the paper.

moments.title: Enquire note-linking program at CERN
moments.detail: A program for typed notes joined by links, written for a CERN Norsk Data computer. Named after a Victorian household manual, later lost on a floppy disk.

moments.title: US defence adopts IP as first major user
moments.detail: The packet-based protocol of Cerf and Kahn. The book gives 1981 only for this adoption, and it says packet switching drew on queuing theory.

moments.title: First Domain Name System registration
moments.detail: Human names for IP addresses, proposed in the early 1980s. The first registered name was symbolics.com in 1985.

moments.title: Steve Jobs forced out of Apple
moments.detail: After a boardroom coup Jobs started NeXT, whose workstation would later be used to build the web.

moments.title: SGML markup language
moments.detail: The document markup used at CERN, which HTML borrowed from to look familiar.

moments.title: Apple releases HyperCard
moments.detail: Linked virtual cards bundled with the Macintosh made hypertext widely popular. Berners-Lee says he had never used it.

moments.title: CERN settles the protocol war on TCP/IP
moments.detail: Ben Segal won the long internal battle against OSI, and by 1988 all at CERN had internet email addresses.

moments.title: Idea of joining hypertext and the internet
moments.detail: Around 1988 Berners-Lee conceived of hypertext links as a simple way to navigate the internet.

moments.title: ACM floppy disk journal on hypertext
moments.detail: An electronic ACM journal issue was the first hypertext Berners-Lee met, probably shared by Cailliau. Its links stayed inside one system.

moments.title: Mesh memo proposes a global hypertext system
moments.detail: A memo with a concept graph titled Mesh argued CERN was a miniature of problems the wider world would face.

moments.title: CERN buys a NeXTcube as a cover for the work
moments.detail: Sendall could not fund Mesh directly, so he proposed trying a NeXT computer. Its development tools then made the first web software practical.

moments.title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol designed
moments.detail: A new protocol like FTP but quick and hidden from the user, written from about October 1990.

moments.title: Universal identifiers for anything on the web
moments.detail: Links named as Universal Document Identifiers, borrowing the double slash from Apollo workstations. Berners-Lee thought them the most important part of the web.

moments.title: Hypertext Markup Language defined
moments.detail: A simple page format based largely on SGML, which CERN documentation systems already used. Berners-Lee did not expect people to write it by hand.

moments.title: Design Issues notes begin
moments.detail: Public hypertext notes on the challenges of the web, kept up for thirty-five years. Berners-Lee considers them the first blog.

moments.title: Mesh memo reissued at a manager's request
moments.detail: After no action, a manager asked about the project and Berners-Lee sent the same memo again with both dates.

moments.title: First web client, a read and write tool
moments.detail: A browser and editor for NeXT, finished by 13 December and versioned as Christmas Day 1990. The first web software totalled 9,555 lines of Objective-C.

moments.title: First web server on the office NeXTcube
moments.detail: The server software ran on a single machine, which carried a warning sticker against switching it off.

moments.title: First web page explaining the project
moments.detail: A monochrome page on info.cern.ch telling people about the web and how to join it.

moments.title: Universal command-line browser
moments.detail: Nicola Pellow wrote a read-only client that ran on almost any computer. Links were footnoted and followed by number.

moments.title: CERN phone book served over the web
moments.detail: By mid-1991 around a thousand staff used the web, mostly for phone numbers, which gave them a reason to install a browser.

moments.title: First website outside CERN at SLAC
moments.detail: Kunz and Addis put scientific papers online in HTML. It proved the web useful to physicists and eased tension at CERN.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Gopher menu-driven internet protocol
moments.detail: A campus information system and chief rival of the web. More people used it than the web until 1994.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Web demo at the Hypertext 91 conference
moments.detail: Cailliau improvised a phone line and power so they could show the web in San Antonio, with Engelbart among the attendees.

moments.title: US Congress funds the Information Superhighway
moments.detail: A bill led by Al Gore allotted about $600 million, encouraged early browsers and paid for the Mosaic team.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Web announced on the alt.hypertext newsgroup
moments.detail: Berners-Lee offered the prototype code by anonymous FTP. The response was lukewarm, yet the post reached Pei-Yuan Wei.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Autodesk drops Xanadu
moments.detail: On the day Berners-Lee first met Nelson, Autodesk returned the project to its informal developers.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: ViolaWWW browser for X Window
moments.detail: Pei-Yuan Wei added bookmarks, history, navigation buttons, applets and style sheets, features Berners-Lee says became standard in later browsers.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Berners-Lee loses the Universal naming fight at IETF
moments.detail: At San Diego the working group chose Uniform over Universal. Berners-Lee thought Uniform implied conformity and still uses his term.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Cello, first Windows browser
moments.detail: Tom Bruce moved his Legal Information Institute from Gopher to the web and began this browser, whose name riffed on Viola.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Wizard's Workshop, first web meet-up
moments.detail: Held in Cambridge, Massachusetts in summer 1993 by Dale Dougherty. Berners-Lee thought Andreessen kept his distance there.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Global News Network web publication
moments.detail: The first commercial web publication, launched through the Wizard's Workshop and remembered for the first clickable advertisement.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Mosaic ported to Windows
moments.detail: Arriving shortly after summer 1993, the port set off a flood of public interest and gave Mosaic a commanding lead.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Hypertext 93 conference is all about the web
moments.detail: In Seattle, every project shown touched the web, a reversal from the 1991 conference.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Myst computer game
moments.detail: Game whose door-based 3-D navigation suggested how the web might be moved through.

moments.title: First clickable web advertisement
moments.detail: Tech publisher O'Reilly served a clickable ad that was essentially a button.

moments.title: Markey bill auctions US mobile spectrum
moments.detail: Legislation created licences for seven new providers, opening cellular service to competition, and prices fell.

moments.title: Mosaic browser released for testing
moments.detail: A Unix browser from NCSA with fast releases and a What's New page, whose team was funded through the Gore bill. Hardin seemed to see it as a sequel to his Collage.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Andreessen proposes inline images in HTML
moments.detail: Berners-Lee wanted a more general link for media. After a debate joined by van Rossum, Andreessen simply added the tag to Mosaic.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Minnesota reserves the right to charge for Gopher
moments.detail: The backlash cut Gopher use and lifted the web, and pushed Berners-Lee to seek a free release of the web.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: Tense meeting with the Mosaic team at NCSA
moments.detail: Berners-Lee objected to rebranding the web as Mosaic. His suggestion of an editor was called impossible, and Andreessen and Hardin seemed at odds over credit.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: CERN gives up all rights to the web code
moments.detail: After lobbying by Berners-Lee and Cailliau, Hoogland agreed, and CERN published the source code with a signed release of rights.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: First New York Times mention of the web
moments.detail: The article focused on Mosaic and pictured Hardin and Smarr. It showed the web gaining momentum, though Andreessen and Bina went unnamed.
moments.ref: Chapter 4: The Rise of the Web

moments.title: The public arrives through AOL
moments.detail: AOL opened the net to the public, ending academic netiquette and bringing a wave of amateur sites.

moments.title: A web of data computers can read
moments.detail: In his WWW1 closing speech Berners-Lee described moving from documents to structured data computers could reason about.

moments.title: Virtual Reality Markup Language
moments.detail: Standard meant to let people walk between web sites through virtual doors; it never caught on as hoped.

moments.title: Bezos settles on online bookselling
moments.detail: Driving from New York to Seattle about when Berners-Lee reached New England, Bezos chose to sell books on the web.

moments.title: Netscape Navigator launches
moments.detail: Follow-up to Mosaic by Andreessen and his NCSA team with Jim Clark; leading browser by mid-1995.

moments.title: Gates buys Spyglass
moments.detail: Microsoft bought the NCSA spin-off in late 1994, intending a browser of its own to extend Windows.

moments.title: Yahoo topic directory
moments.detail: Two Stanford students began a hand-maintained directory of web pages by topic, with no search at first.

moments.title: Justin Hall personal site
moments.detail: A Swarthmore freshman documented his life on the web, in what Berners-Lee calls perhaps the first blog with comments.

moments.title: Zurich talk on a web consortium
moments.detail: Berners-Lee and Dertouzos discussed how a web organization might work, with the MIT X Windows consortium as template.

moments.title: Arena browser shown at WWW1
moments.detail: Raggett showed a browser with background images, tables and text flow, many of which entered the HTML roadmap. Dated by the conference.

moments.title: Interactive web map viewer
moments.detail: Xerox PARC tool that generated maps on demand. Dated by its prize, not its release.

moments.title: Virtual copy of the Louvre
moments.detail: A French student digitized the museum online. Dated by its prize, not its release.

moments.title: World Wide Web Worm
moments.detail: One of the first search engines, coded at the University of Colorado. Dated by its prize, not its release.

moments.title: First web conference at CERN
moments.detail: About 350 people met at CERN, after a standoff with NCSA over who would go first; HTML and HTTP roadmaps took shape.

moments.title: First Best of the Web prizes
moments.detail: Prizes voted by email went to a map viewer, a virtual Louvre and a search engine at the WWW1 dinner.

moments.title: MIT agrees to host W3C
moments.detail: Vezza phoned with the go-ahead for hiring Berners-Lee and giving space and funding to the consortium, modelled on the X Consortium contract.

moments.title: Berners-Lee starts at MIT
moments.detail: Berners-Lee left CERN and Europe for Boston, keeping a French link through INRIA.

moments.title: Gates memo on the internet
moments.detail: Gates told executives the internet was the most important development since the IBM PC; the strategy became embrace and extend.

moments.title: Internet Explorer debuts
moments.detail: A rushed first release bundled with Windows that later took about 95 per cent of the market by 2002.

moments.title: First browser war begins
moments.detail: Netscape and Microsoft fought in the market and inside W3C, adding browser-specific features. Berners-Lee counts it as the second war.

moments.title: Third-party ad network
moments.detail: Banner ads served across sites with tracked click-through rates and shared revenue.

moments.title: Grail browser in Python
moments.detail: A browser that ran applications inside itself using Python; Berners-Lee urged it on but would not push Python in W3C.

moments.title: Rapidly editable wiki pages
moments.detail: Cunningham invented them and did not patent the concept, thinking nobody would pay for it.

moments.title: HTML2 standard
moments.detail: Next version of HTML in the W3C sequence.

moments.title: Netscape goes public
moments.detail: Oversubscribed share sale that surprised Berners-Lee, since Netscape had no obvious way to make money.

moments.title: Keio becomes third W3C host
moments.detail: W3C added a Tokyo host to handle growing interest from Asia.

moments.title: Cascading Style Sheets standard
moments.detail: Lie designed a cascade of style rules, tested with Bos on the Arena browser; W3C published the first standard.

moments.title: Craigslist local listings
moments.detail: Web mailing list of San Francisco events that spread to listings and cities worldwide.

moments.title: New York Times goes online
moments.detail: The paper began posting its text on the web, a sign of the slow shift from print to digital.

moments.title: US Telecommunications Act and Section 230
moments.detail: Its obscenity language was later struck down; its safe harbour clause later proved crucial to social media.

moments.title: Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace
moments.detail: Barlow manifesto against government rule online. Berners-Lee had mixed feelings and thought offline law still applied.

moments.title: Alexa Internet traffic rankings
moments.detail: For-profit analysis of web traffic and page popularity, sold to Amazon in 1999.

moments.title: Internet Archive begins snapshotting the web
moments.detail: Kahle saw pages were short-lived and began regular copies, first held on a tape robot.

moments.title: Microsoft ActiveX
moments.detail: Browser components for video and games. Berners-Lee thought their one notable trait was being incompatible with Netscape.

moments.title: Apple buys NeXT
moments.detail: Apple purchased what remained of NeXT, and Jobs was soon reinstated as CEO.

moments.title: PageRank link analysis
moments.detail: Stanford students ranked pages by the structure of links and lists, not word counts; soon rebranded as Google.

moments.title: HTML3 standard
moments.detail: Next version of HTML in the W3C sequence.

moments.title: W3C accessibility standards effort
moments.detail: Brewer joined to lead accessibility standards, and every W3C spec came to get an accessibility review. Dated by her joining.

moments.title: Akamai incorporated
moments.detail: Lewin and Leighton turned consistent hashing, a fix for sudden traffic overload, into a content distribution business.

moments.title: Extensible Markup Language
moments.detail: W3C standard simpler than HTML and built to carry abstract data as well as documents; Microsoft adopted it widely.

moments.title: Jon Postel dies
moments.detail: Death of the long-time custodian of the name registry, whose legacy Berners-Lee thought was betrayed by a for-profit registry.

moments.title: Kahle sells Alexa to Amazon
moments.detail: The sale let Kahle turn to running the Internet Archive full-time.

moments.title: The Cluetrain Manifesto
moments.detail: Early document of ninety-five theses, coauthored by Searls, that predicted the impact of the web on business and marketing.

moments.title: LiveJournal
moments.detail: An early web community.

moments.title: HTTPS agreed
moments.detail: Encrypted web traffic using RSA; changing the URL prefix broke existing links.

moments.title: HTML4 standard
moments.detail: Next version of HTML in the W3C sequence.

moments.title: Pets.com goes bankrupt
moments.detail: The standard-bearer of the dot-com bubble collapsed amid hundreds of similar firms.

moments.title: Wayback Machine opens
moments.detail: Kahle opened the Internet Archive database of web snapshots to the public.

moments.title: Mac OS X, adopted at W3C
moments.detail: W3C switched to it soon after its arrival; Berners-Lee saw NeXT in its design.

moments.title: AOL Time Warner write-down
moments.detail: A 50 billion dollar write-down after which Netscape dwindled and the web bubble burst.

moments.title: Wikipedia launches
moments.detail: Open encyclopaedia grown out of Nupedia; Berners-Lee calls it probably the best example of what he wanted the web to be.

moments.title: Michael Dertouzos dies
moments.detail: Loss of the friend, mentor and main supporter of Berners-Lee at MIT.

moments.title: Daniel Lewin killed on Flight 11
moments.detail: The Akamai CTO died in the 9/11 attacks, probably while trying to stop the hijackers.

moments.title: Explorer reaches 95 per cent share
moments.detail: With Netscape in shambles, the browser wars looked over to outsiders.

moments.title: Last.fm spun off from Southampton
moments.detail: Music service that matched listening habits across users. It was where Berners-Lee first met collaborative filtering.

moments.title: Friendster
moments.detail: An early social network.

moments.title: W3C royalty-free patent policy
moments.detail: A group led by Weitzner wrote it after a royalty claim scare; Berners-Lee says it saved the web.

moments.title: MIT reunites its computer science and AI labs
moments.detail: The labs had long been separate, partly because scientists distanced themselves from AI during the funding drought.

moments.title: Google buys Applied Semantics
moments.detail: Gil Elbaz sold his semantic start-up to Google for more than 100 million dollars. It provided the core of AdSense.

moments.title: Myspace
moments.detail: An early social network.

moments.title: HTML5, the WHATWG flavour
moments.detail: Tolerant of errors and powerful for applications; W3C ultimately endorsed it. Dated by the start of WHATWG work.

moments.title: Mozilla launches Firefox
moments.detail: Alternative browser that wore down the Explorer monopoly from the mid-2000s; the browser Berners-Lee used most.

moments.title: Gmail built with AJAX
moments.detail: Web mail that felt always on through background data loading.

moments.title: Google passes Yahoo in search
moments.detail: Google became the dominant search engine, a new monopoly forming as the Explorer one faded.

moments.title: Facebook
moments.detail: Started at Harvard and built on the communities before it.

moments.title: WHATWG breaks from W3C
moments.detail: After losing a W3C vote, Mozilla, Opera and Apple representatives formed a splinter group. Berners-Lee thought it the first real blow to the integrity of the web.

moments.title: Google Maps
moments.detail: AJAX map application that kept data on the device to seem always on.

moments.title: W3C starts the Mobile Web Initiative
moments.detail: A W3C effort led by Hoschka to prepare websites for phones, including touch events, more than two years before the iPhone.

moments.title: First W3C China office
moments.detail: Opened at Beihang University; Angel Li pushed for open standards there.

moments.title: The intention economy
moments.detail: Doc Searls coined it: buyers state what they want and vendors compete, as an alternative to the attention economy. Berners-Lee adopted the framing and discussed it with John Bruce on CNBC in 2023.

moments.title: Apple launches the iPhone
moments.detail: Jobs first showcased its Safari browser. Berners-Lee later came to see the app store around it as gatekeeping.

moments.title: Berners-Lee testifies on net neutrality
moments.detail: Testified to the US House at the request of Markey, arguing for equal treatment of data packets.

moments.title: Google Chrome launches
moments.detail: Instant hit helped by close fit with HTML5. Berners-Lee thought Hickson had quietly steered HTML towards the needs of Chrome.

moments.title: RECAP frees US court records
moments.detail: Swartz and others scraped nearly 20 million pages from the paid PACER database into a free archive. The FBI looked into it but filed no charges.

moments.title: Common Crawl web archive
moments.detail: Nonprofit monthly copy of the web, about 50 billion pages. The data set that made GPT work, though it holds much copyrighted text.

moments.title: Spotify
moments.detail: Followed Last.fm in recommending music from what similar listeners played.

moments.title: TED talk calls for Raw Data Now
moments.detail: First of two TED talks showing the power of publishing open government data on the web.

moments.title: Privacy warning at Westminster
moments.detail: Told UK parliamentarians that click data reveals intimate facts and should not be collected at all.

moments.title: Data.gov.uk launches
moments.detail: UK open government data site that followed the advice of Berners-Lee to Gordon Brown, with Shadbolt suggested as lead.

moments.title: Web Foundation launches
moments.detail: Launched in Washington with Knight Foundation money, aiming to bring 3 billion more people online by 2019.

moments.title: Google leaves China
moments.detail: No agreement with the government on censoring results; Baidu took over.

moments.title: East Africa tour on affordable access
moments.detail: Meetings with officials led Berners-Lee to see avoiding broadband monopolies as the key issue.

moments.title: New UK government cancels the project
moments.detail: After Labour lost the election, Cameron immediately cancelled the project, and Shadbolt and Berners-Lee had to argue their case again.

moments.title: DeepMind founded
moments.detail: Hassabis, Legg and Suleyman set out to build a general artificial intelligence.

moments.title: Lunch with Larry Page on AI
moments.detail: Berners-Lee asked about a stream of consciousness in code; Page offered to run it if someone wrote it.

moments.title: Arab Spring begins in Tunisia
moments.detail: Protests coordinated on Twitter and Facebook spread across the region. Berners-Lee calls it the first large demonstration that social media would transform society.

moments.title: Nilekani explains the paper problem
moments.detail: On the Hyderabad trip, Nilekani said records had to go digital first, the job of the Aadhaar ID program.

moments.title: WebRTC first working draft
moments.detail: W3C draft for in-browser real-time communication. First cross-browser call in 2013, official standard in 2017; Zoom, Google Meet, Teams and Jitsi use it, and usage surged during Covid.

moments.title: THIS IS FOR EVERYONE at the Olympics
moments.detail: At the ceremony directed by Boyle, Berners-Lee typed the phrase on a NeXT machine; it ran around the stadium and went out as a tweet.

moments.title: Open Data Institute founded
moments.detail: A UK government grant of 10 million pounds started the nonprofit, won by Berners-Lee and Shadbolt with help from Willets.

moments.title: Beihang becomes fourth W3C host
moments.detail: The Beijing office grew into a full host alongside Japan, France and the US.

moments.title: Aaron Swartz dies during prosecution
moments.detail: He took his own life after plea talks collapsed on charges over bulk JSTOR downloads through MIT. Berners-Lee thought the charges disproportionate.

moments.title: Web Foundation publishes the Web Index
moments.detail: Pilot ranking of countries by access, freedom, openness and content, used to direct the policy work of the foundation.

moments.title: Hassabis shows neural nets at web anniversary
moments.detail: At a Google dinner for the Web Foundation, Berners-Lee first met Hassabis and first saw how such systems learn without explicit logic layers.

moments.title: MasterCard funds Solid research at MIT
moments.detail: A gift of $1 million paid for further work and a prototype of the first Solid server.

moments.title: ODI supports Burkina Faso election
moments.detail: A mobile web app on an open data portal delivered results from twenty-one districts within hours.

moments.title: Polis sets Taiwan ride-sharing policy
moments.detail: Citizens reached a consensus on regulating Uber through the Polis app, which Berners-Lee admires for promoting the norm over extremes.

moments.title: Solid: personal data pods
moments.detail: Web servers that hold a person's own data, for apps to read and write with consent. The book first dates the work to the 2015 MasterCard gift.

moments.title: AlphaGo beats a Go world champion
moments.detail: DeepMind neural network that became the first computer to defeat a human world champion at Go.

moments.title: Berners-Lee wins the Turing Award
moments.detail: Top computing prize from the ACM, presented months later at a San Francisco banquet attended by Cerf.

moments.title: Brexit campaign narrowcasts on social media
moments.detail: Berners-Lee thought targeted messaging, aided by Cambridge Analytica, was one cause of the result and the first sign of serious trouble.

moments.title: Trump elected amid targeted propaganda
moments.detail: Cambridge Analytica worked to influence US voters. Berners-Lee thought its role perhaps overstated but saw the danger of secret targeting.

moments.title: Mastodon
moments.detail: Protocol-based social network with many independent servers; preferred by Berners-Lee.

moments.title: AlphaZero tops computer chess
moments.detail: Successor to AlphaGo, it became the strongest chess computer in existence.

moments.title: Charlie, an AI that works for you
moments.detail: A note imagining a personal agent with deep access to the data of its user, answering to that user and not big tech.

moments.title: Equifax data breach
moments.detail: Hackers took personal data of over 147 million people, an example of the legal liability central data stores create.

moments.title: Google transformer architecture
moments.detail: Neural net architecture from a Google research team, adopted by OpenAI.

moments.title: Berners-Lee starts Inrupt
moments.detail: After years in nonprofits he decided a funded company was needed to build Solid at scale, then registered the corporation and recruited John Bruce as CEO.

moments.title: EU privacy law takes effect
moments.detail: Toughest privacy law in the world and a boost to the case for Solid. Berners-Lee thought its cookie rules were overdone and caused annoying consent pop-ups because legislators did not consult W3C.

moments.title: Turing Prize for AI research
moments.detail: Awarded to LeCun, Bengio and Hinton. Only LeCun is comfortable with AI risk.

moments.title: ActivityPub
moments.detail: W3C standard protocol behind Mastodon.

moments.title: GPT models
moments.detail: OpenAI trained the transformer first on e-books (GPT-1) with poor results, then on web data; GPT-3 and later models shocked researchers.

moments.title: AlphaFold
moments.detail: Protein structure prediction, drawing on the work on Go and chess.

moments.title: Rosemary Leith speech on inclusion and AI
moments.detail: At Kirkcaldy she named AI as a major coming force and argued that the invisible hand should give way to an inclusive hand.
moments.ref: Chapter 14: The Contract for the Web

moments.title: Thirtieth birthday tour of the web
moments.detail: A day of events at CERN, Downing Street and the Science Museum, then Lagos, followed by Kirkcaldy. Berners-Lee reported on the state of the web and voiced worry about darker forces.
moments.ref: Chapter 14: The Contract for the Web

moments.title: Contract for the Web announced
moments.detail: Web Foundation text announced at CERN. A working group with Google, Microsoft, Wikimedia, Germany and France settled nine principles split among governments, companies and citizens; about eighty firms signed. Non-binding. Agreement took months after the announcement.
moments.ref: Chapter 14: The Contract for the Web

moments.title: The Social Dilemma released
moments.detail: Film from Harris on engagement algorithms. Berners-Lee recommends it but thought it only points out the problem.

moments.title: Citizen data pods in Flanders
moments.detail: Minister-president Jan Jambon announced that citizens would deal with government through pods. The joint venture Athumi runs them for about six million people.

moments.title: Marcos uses social media in Philippine election
moments.detail: He avoided traditional journalism and used Facebook and TikTok to whitewash the record of his parents, an example of the global problem.

moments.title: Ditchley summit on AI
moments.detail: Technologists, strategists and politicians met after ChatGPT appeared. Berners-Lee tried out his idea of an AI that works for the user, as a doctor or lawyer does.

moments.title: ChatGPT debuts
moments.detail: Public chat portal to OpenAI models. Berners-Lee calls it a step change for the web, comparable to RSA and PageRank.

moments.title: First global AI safety summit
moments.detail: The UK convened it at Bletchley Park, with Rishi Sunak, Kamala Harris, Elon Musk and Wu Zhaohui attending.

moments.title: W3C becomes a nonprofit corporation
moments.detail: It left the hosted model for a Delaware corporation with a board of directors; technical decisions stayed with working groups.

moments.title: Berners-Lee steps down as W3C director
moments.detail: A long phase-out ended and he became director emeritus and a non-voting board member, to focus on Solid and Inrupt.

moments.title: Andreessen essay on AI optimism
moments.detail: His blog dismissed killer robot fears. Berners-Lee thought he could not imagine something smarter than himself.

moments.title: New York Times sues OpenAI
moments.detail: Copyright suit against OpenAI and Microsoft over articles used to train GPT and reproduced by it.

moments.title: W3C moves from Twitter to Mastodon
moments.detail: The consortium left X for Mastodon, whose protocol ActivityPub is a W3C standard.

moments.title: Hassabis wins Nobel for AlphaFold
moments.detail: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized neural net prediction of protein shapes.

moments.title: Browsers drop third-party cookies
moments.detail: By late 2024 Firefox and Safari no longer allowed invasive tracking cookies, while Chrome had not followed.

moments.title: GPT passes a Stanford Turing test
moments.detail: Researchers found the chatbot output statistically indistinguishable from tens of thousands of humans. Berners-Lee credits open web data.

moments.title: Call for a CERN style AI institution
moments.detail: Demis Hassabis called for a shared global institution for AI researchers; Berners-Lee supports the idea.

moments.title: AI summit in Seoul
moments.detail: A follow-up to Bletchley with more focus on innovation.

moments.title: Microsoft hires the Inflection team
moments.detail: Mustafa Suleyman and most of his team left Inflection for Microsoft, after Berners-Lee had pitched pairing its AI with Solid.

moments.title: US rule on reasonable data formats
moments.detail: A US regulation requiring data to be available in a reasonable form, which Berners-Lee sees as top-down support for Solid.

moments.title: Charlie AI demonstrated at Inrupt
moments.detail: Internal demo of a personal AI using a private pod of simulated data, which gave far better advice with consent than without.

moments.title: Berners-Lee endorses McCourt bid for TikTok
moments.detail: The consortium aimed to buy the US assets of TikTok and retrain its algorithms for quality of life, not time on device.

moments.title: A Map of Everything on the Internet
moments.detail: Design Issues diagram sorting open systems from harmful ones that flow into feed manipulation for engagement.

moments.title: US surgeon general seeks social media warning
moments.detail: Murthy asked for a warning label like those on cigarettes, citing adolescent mental health figures.

moments.title: Web Foundation wind down announced
moments.detail: Berners-Lee and Rosemary Leith cited a mission partly met and judged that reducing social media toxicity was beyond its scope.

moments.title: AI Action Summit in Paris
moments.detail: Co-chaired by Emmanuel Macron and Narendra Modi. Berners-Lee thought the shift from safety to action meant less work on guardrails.

moments.title: Make It Fair protest by artists
moments.detail: Artists including Kate Bush released a silent album against a UK proposal to let AI firms train on creative work unless creators opted out.
